title: Racing Against the Storm
summary: A fishing family races to bring their boats ashore and secure their property before an approaching storm hits, with the children taking on real responsibilities to help.
poll: Children should be given real responsibilities, even during an emergency.

versions.title: Racing Against the Storm
versions.text:
Maha lives by the sea. Her dad has three boats. His name is Rashid.

One day, the radio warns of a storm. It will come at night. The wind will be strong.

Dad calls the family. "We must work fast," he says. They pull the boats up on the sand. They tie them down with rope.

Maha ties good knots on the rope. Her small brother, Fahad, carries boxes and nets. They work as a team.

The sky turns dark. The wind gets strong. Mom shuts the windows. She gets food and a flashlight.

Dad checks an old man's boat, too. He ties it down. Maha and Fahad help him.

They finish just in time. The wind howls. Rain falls hard. The family goes in, safe and dry.

In the morning, the storm is gone. The boats are safe. Dad feels proud. Maha and Fahad helped a lot.

Father calls the family together. "We must work fast," he says. They must pull the boats onto the sand. They must tie them down with rope.

Maha ties strong knots on the ropes. Her little brother, Fahad, carries boxes and nets to a safe place. Everyone works as a team.

The sky grows dark. The wind picks up. Mother closes all the windows. She gets food, water, and a flashlight ready.

Father checks an old neighbor's boat, too. He ties it down. Maha and Fahad help him.

They finish just as the storm starts. The wind howls. Rain pours down hard. The family goes inside, safe and dry.

In the morning, the storm has passed. All the boats are safe. Father feels proud. Maha and Fahad worked hard to help.

versions.title: Racing Against the Storm
versions.text:
Maha's family has fished along this coast for many years. Her father, Rashid, owns three small fishing boats with her uncles, and they go out to sea nearly every day.

One afternoon, the radio gives a warning: a powerful storm is coming and will reach the coast by evening, bringing strong wind and large waves.

Father quickly gathers the family. "We must prepare right now," he says. There is little time left. They need to haul the boats onto the sand and secure them tightly with heavy rope.

Maha's job is to tie strong, careful knots on every rope. Her younger brother, Fahad, carries boxes of gear and nets to a safe shelter away from the shore. Everyone works as a team, racing against the darkening sky.

As the wind grows stronger, Mother secures the house. She closes every window, brings in the outdoor furniture, and gathers food, water, and a flashlight.

Father also checks on an old neighbor's boat, helping secure it the same careful way. Maha and Fahad help him finish the job before the rain starts.

They finish just as the first drops fall. The wind howls outside, and heavy rain pours down for hours. Safe inside, the family listens to the storm.

By morning, the storm has passed. Every boat along the shore is safe, thanks to their hard work. Father praises Maha and Fahad for working so hard to protect the family's boats.

They finish just as the first heavy drops begin to fall steadily; the wind howls relentlessly outside, and heavy rain pours down for many hours without any sign whatsoever of relenting, while safe inside their sturdy shelter, the family listens anxiously to the storm raging on throughout the long, uneasy night.

By morning, the storm has finally passed entirely, leaving the village remarkably unharmed despite its considerable fury, and every boat along the shore remains safe, thanks largely to the forecast's timely warning and everyone's diligent, well-coordinated hard work; Father praises Maha and Fahad warmly for taking their responsibilities so seriously and for helping protect both their immediate family and their broader, interconnected community.

versions.title: Racing Against the Storm
versions.text:
Maha's family has fished along this stretch of coast for many generations, since fishing has always constituted their community's primary and most essential means of livelihood, meticulously passed down from parent to child across the decades; her father, Rashid, owns three small fishing boats together with her uncles, and collectively they venture out to sea nearly every single day in order to earn their living from the unpredictable waters surrounding their village.

One afternoon, the local weather forecast issues an urgent, unmistakable warning: a powerful, rapidly intensifying storm is approaching and will reach the coast by evening, bringing dangerously strong winds and large, unpredictable waves capable of damaging anything left unsecured along the exposed shoreline.

Father quickly gathers the entire family together, insisting that they must prepare immediately, since their modest boats remain especially vulnerable once the storm actually makes landfall; they need to haul the boats onto the sand and anchor them securely with heavy rope before it becomes too late to act responsibly and effectively.

Maha willingly assumes the responsibility of tying strong, meticulously careful knots on every single rope, determined not to leave anything whatsoever to chance, while her younger brother, Fahad, meanwhile carries boxes of gear and fishing nets to a safe shelter situated well away from the exposed shore; everyone in the family works diligently together as a cohesive team, racing against the increasingly darkening, threatening sky overhead.

As the wind grows noticeably stronger and the temperature drops considerably, Mother secures the house with equal, methodical care, closing every window, bringing in the outdoor furniture, and gathering food, water, and a flashlight in case the electricity fails unexpectedly during the long, uncertain night ahead.

Father also checks on an elderly neighbor's boat, recognizing that it remains just as vulnerable to the approaching storm as their own family's property, and he feels a genuine, unshakable sense of responsibility to help protect it, since helping one another is simply an essential, deeply ingrained, longstanding part of life within their tight-knit coastal community; Maha and Fahad gladly assist in securing it as well, without being asked twice, exactly as they have been taught since early childhood.

questions.stem: Why does Mother bring in the outdoor furniture?
options: She is cleaning the yard and the garden for the guests
She wants to sell it at the market this weekend
It is too hot outside, so the chairs would get burned
Strong wind could blow it around and cause damage
questions.why: Since a storm with strong wind is coming, loose furniture outside could be blown around and cause damage.

wrong.A: The article does not mention cleaning.
wrong.B: The article never mentions selling furniture.
wrong.C: The article describes a storm, not hot weather.

questions.stem: Why does Father check on the elderly neighbor's boat as well as his own?
options: He is required to by the radio station, which tells all fishermen to do it
He cares about his neighbor and believes in helping others in the community
He wants to be paid for the help, since the neighbor is a rich man
He has no boats of his own to protect, so he checks his neighbor's boat
questions.why: Father secures his own boats first, then helps his neighbor simply because he cares about others nearby.

wrong.A: The radio only gives a weather warning.
wrong.C: The article never mentions payment.
wrong.D: Father already owns and secures three boats of his own.

questions.stem: What is the result of the family's careful preparation before the storm?
options: The boats are damaged anyway by the waves
The family loses their home to the water
Nothing changes for the boats or the family
All the boats stay safe through the storm
questions.why: Because the family prepared so carefully, every boat along the shore stays safe through the storm.

wrong.A: The article says the boats are safe, not damaged.
wrong.B: The article never mentions losing the home.
wrong.C: The preparation clearly makes a difference in keeping the boats safe.

questions.stem: How does the author organize most of the article?
options: By following the events in the order they happen, from the warning to the morning after
By comparing two different storms that hit the coast, one after the other in the same year
By listing facts about different fish that live near the shore, from the smallest to the largest
By explaining how boats are built, and then how sailors keep them safe from the waves
questions.why: The article moves through events in order: the warning, preparing, the storm itself, and the calm morning after.

wrong.B: The article describes only one storm.
wrong.C: The article does not list fish facts.
wrong.D: The article does not explain boat building.

MID.prompt: Explain how the family worked together to prepare for the storm. Use at least two details from the article.
checklist: I explained how the family worked together.
I used at least two details from the article.
I organized my ideas in a clear order.
MID.modelAnswer: The family worked together to prepare quickly for the storm. After hearing the warning on the radio, Maha tied careful knots on every rope while Fahad carried gear and nets to a safe shelter. Mother secured the house by closing the windows and gathering supplies. Father even helped secure an elderly neighbor's boat. Because everyone did their part, all of the boats stayed safe through the storm.

keyWords.definition: a statement about what the weather will probably be like in the near future
keyWords.example: The forecast predicted rain for the entire weekend.

keyWords.definition: to fix something firmly in place so it does not drift or move
keyWords.example: The sailors anchored the boat near the quiet beach.

keyWords.definition: a duty or job that a person is expected to take care of
keyWords.example: Feeding the class fish was Omar's responsibility every Friday.

keyWords.definition: a group of people who live in the same area and often help one another
keyWords.example: The whole community helped clean up the park after the festival.

keyWords.definition: easily hurt, damaged, or affected by something
keyWords.example: Young plants are vulnerable to frost in early spring.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the central idea of the article?
options: A storm proves beyond any doubt that fishing boats can never truly be protected from severe, dangerous weather, no matter how carefully a family tries to prepare in advance.
Children should always stay inside during a storm.
A family moves away from the coast permanently.
A family that relies on fishing uses forecast warnings, responsibility, and teamwork to protect their property and their community from a storm.
questions.why: The article shows the family using the forecast warning, dividing responsibilities, and helping a neighbor to protect their boats and their community.

wrong.A: The boats stay safe because of the family's preparation.
wrong.B: The children, Maha and Fahad, are given real outdoor tasks, not kept inside.
wrong.C: The article never mentions the family moving away.

questions.stem: According to the article, why does Father say the family's boats are vulnerable?
options: They are small and could easily be damaged by the approaching storm
They are too old to use
They are kept very far away from home for storage during most of the season
They are far too heavy and bulky for anyone to move alone
questions.why: In the article, the family's small boats remain especially vulnerable once the storm arrives.

wrong.B: The article never says the boats are too old.
wrong.C: The boats are kept near their home village.
wrong.D: The family is able to haul the boats onto the sand.

questions.stem: What specific task does Maha take responsibility for?
options: Forecasting the weather
Carefully repairing the neighbor's old house roof after the storm
Tying careful, strong knots on every rope
Steering a boat out to sea
questions.why: In the article, Maha takes on the responsibility of tying strong, careful knots on every single rope.

wrong.A: The radio station gives the forecast, not Maha.
wrong.B: The article does not mention repairing a house.
wrong.D: No one steers a boat out to sea in the article.

questions.stem: In the article, the word vulnerable means —
options: completely safe from any harm
extremely valuable
very far away
easily harmed or damaged
questions.why: The article describes the small boats as vulnerable, meaning they could easily be damaged by the storm.

wrong.A: Vulnerable means the opposite of safe.
wrong.B: The word describes risk, not worth.
wrong.C: The word describes danger, not distance.

questions.stem: Why does Father feel a responsibility to help secure his elderly neighbor's boat?
options: Helping others is simply part of life in their close-knit community
The neighbor threatens to report him if he refuses to help
He is paid a fee for the help by the harbor office each month
The radio forecast orders him to do it before the storm arrives
questions.why: In the story, helping each other is a normal part of life in their coastal community.

wrong.B: The article never mentions any threat.
wrong.C: The article never mentions payment.
wrong.D: The forecast only reports the coming weather.

questions.stem: What can readers infer about the family from how quickly and calmly they prepare for the storm?
options: They have never experienced a storm before, so they are learning as they go
They panic and do not know what to do, so they argue about the boats
They do not care about their boats and leave them out in the open sea
They are experienced and know how to handle this kind of danger together
questions.why: The family moves efficiently through clear tasks without confusion, suggesting they have prepared for storms before.

wrong.A: Their calm, organized response suggests real experience.
wrong.B: The family stays calm and organized rather than panicking.
wrong.C: Their hard work to protect the boats shows they care deeply.

questions.stem: How are Maha's and her father's actions during the story alike?
options: Both ignore the storm forecast and stay at home, safe inside the house
Both refuse to help anyone outside the family at all, even in danger
Both take responsibility for securing boats, their own and a neighbor's
Both are afraid to go near the shore of the sea, so they stay far away
questions.why: Maha ties knots on the family's ropes, and Father secures both his own boats and a neighbor's, showing both take real responsibility.

wrong.A: Both act immediately because of the forecast warning.
wrong.B: Father helps a neighbor, and Maha helps too without being asked.
wrong.D: Both work directly on the shore to secure the boats.

questions.stem: Why does the author include the detail that Father also secures an elderly neighbor's boat, beyond his own family's boats?
options: To emphasize that responsibility in a community extends beyond one's own family
To show that storms only damage old boats, so new boats do not need any rope
To explain how boats are repaired after a storm and who pays for the work
To suggest that neighbors should not be trusted with a family's boats
questions.why: By showing Father helping a neighbor, the author highlights that responsibility in a close community reaches beyond one's own household.

wrong.B: The storm threatens all unsecured boats, not only old ones.
wrong.C: The article does not explain boat repair.
wrong.D: Father's actions show trust and care for his neighbor, not distrust.

HIGH.prompt: Do you think children should be given real responsibilities during an emergency, like Maha and Fahad were? Support your argument with evidence from the article, and address at least one point someone might make against your view.
checklist: I supported my position with specific evidence from the article.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I believe children should be given real responsibilities during an emergency, and the article supports this view. Maha was trusted with the important task of tying strong, careful knots on every rope, and her work helped keep the family's boats safe through the storm. Fahad also took on a real job by carrying gear and nets to a safe shelter. Someone might argue that children could get hurt or make mistakes during a dangerous situation, but the article shows that with clear instructions and teamwork, children like Maha and Fahad can handle real responsibility safely and make a genuine difference.

LOW.stem: What does Mom get ready besides closing the windows?
options: Boats and ropes
New nets for fishing
Food and a flashlight
A map of the sea
LOW.why: In the text, Mom shuts the windows and gets food and a flashlight.

wrong.A: Dad and the family handle the boats and rope.
wrong.B: Fahad carries the nets, not Mom.
wrong.D: No map is in the article.

LOW.stem: Why is the family safe and dry at the end of the night?
options: They finish and go inside in time.
They sail the boats out to sea.
They sleep on the sandy beach.
They ask the old man for help.
LOW.why: The text says they finish just in time and the family goes in, safe and dry.

wrong.B: They pull the boats onto the sand.
wrong.C: The family goes into the house.
wrong.D: Dad helps the old man; the family does not ask him for help.

LOW.stem: In the article, the word howls means —
options: sleeps in the dark
shines very bright
moves very slowly
makes a loud sound
LOW.why: The wind is strong in the storm, so it howls with a loud sound.

wrong.A: Wind in a storm does not sleep.
wrong.B: Wind makes a sound; it does not shine.
wrong.C: The wind is strong, not slow.

LOW.stem: How is Fahad's job different from Maha's job?
options: Fahad ties knots; Maha shuts windows.
Fahad carries gear; Maha ties knots.
Fahad checks boats; Maha cooks food.
Fahad calls Dad; Maha carries nets.
LOW.why: Maha ties good knots on the rope, while Fahad carries boxes and nets.

wrong.A: Maha ties knots; Mom shuts the windows.
wrong.C: Dad checks the boats; Maha does not cook.
wrong.D: Fahad carries nets, but Maha does not.

MID.stem: How often do the family's boats go out to sea?
options: Only once each year
Nearly every day
Only on Fridays
Once each month
MID.why: The text says Father and the uncles go out to sea nearly every day.

wrong.A: Once a year is much less than nearly every day.
wrong.C: The text does not limit fishing to Fridays.
wrong.D: Once a month is much less than nearly every day.

MID.stem: Why must the family move quickly after the radio warning?
options: The uncles are coming home.
The boats are very heavy.
The sea is already calm.
A storm comes by evening.
MID.why: The storm will reach the coast by evening, so there is little time left.

wrong.A: The uncles are not mentioned as returning.
wrong.B: Heavy boats are not the reason for the hurry.
wrong.C: The sea is not calm; a storm is coming.

MID.stem: In the article, the word shelter means —
options: a safe place away from harm
a boat with strong sails
a rope tied in a knot
a warning on the radio
MID.why: Fahad carries the gear to a shelter away from the shore so it stays safe from the storm.

wrong.B: A boat would not keep gear away from the shore.
wrong.C: A rope is for tying boats, not a place.
wrong.D: A warning is a message, not a place.

MID.stem: What is happening just as the family finishes their work?
options: The sun is coming up.
The wind is dying down.
The first drops of rain fall.
The uncles return from sea.
MID.why: The text says they finish just as the first drops fall.

wrong.A: The sky is getting dark, not light.
wrong.B: The wind grows stronger and howls.
wrong.D: The uncles do not return in the article.

HIGH.stem: Why does Mother gather a flashlight along with food and water?
options: To use when the boats go out
To have light in a blackout
To signal the old neighbor
To give to Fahad for work
HIGH.why: She gathers them in case the power goes out.

wrong.A: The boats are pulled onto the sand, not taken out.
wrong.C: No signaling is mentioned.
wrong.D: Fahad carries gear, not a flashlight, in the text.

HIGH.stem: Why does Father also check on an elderly neighbor's boat?
options: He wants to buy the boat
The neighbor asked him for money
It is in danger from the storm too
It is the biggest boat in town
HIGH.why: Father knows the neighbor's boat is just as vulnerable to the coming storm as his own.

wrong.A: Buying the boat is not mentioned.
wrong.B: Money is not mentioned.
wrong.D: The size of the boat is not the reason.

HIGH.stem: What gave the family time to prepare for the storm?
options: The early warning in the forecast
A visit from the old neighbor
The strong wind at noon
A call from the uncles at sea
HIGH.why: In the text, the boats were safe thanks to the forecast's early warning and everyone's hard work.

wrong.B: The neighbor does not warn them; Father helps him.
wrong.C: The wind grows stronger later, after the warning.
wrong.D: The uncles are not said to call.

HIGH.stem: What does the first paragraph suggest about why the family takes the warning so seriously?
options: They enjoy rough weather.
They only fish for fun.
Their boats are their living.
They moved here last year.
HIGH.why: Fishing is the community's main way of life, and the family earns its living from the boats.

wrong.A: The family works to avoid the storm.
wrong.B: The text says they fish to earn their living.
wrong.D: The family has fished here for many generations.
